title: The late Indian masters
hook: Vikramashila and the teachers who later carried Buddhism to Tibet

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nalanda, the monastery that worked like a university. Your line: the great library.

A request arrives at a monastery in eastern India. It comes from the north, from Tibet, and it asks for one teacher by name. The Tibetan histories tell it as a long courtship: messengers, gifts of gold, a refusal, then a second try. The teacher they wanted was a senior monk at the monastery of Vikramashila, known in Tibet as Atisha. His own monastery did not want to give him up, and tradition says it let him go only for a time, expecting him back. In the end he went, crossed the mountains, and taught in Tibet until he died there.
screen: `A REQUEST FROM TIBET.` → `ONE TEACHER, BY NAME.` → `ATISHA OF VIKRAMASHILA.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Vikramashila stood in eastern India, a monastery that tradition says was founded and supported by kings. Like Nalanda, it was a place of study: monks trained in philosophy, debate, meditation and ritual, and its leading teachers were honored by name. Second, the man. Atisha's monastic name was Dipankara Shrijnana. Tradition says he studied with many teachers, in India and, by some accounts, across the sea in a land called Suvarnadvipa, the golden island. Third, the book. In Tibet, Atisha wrote a short work called the Lamp for the Path to Awakening. It sorts practitioners into three kinds of people: those who seek a better life to come, those who seek their own freedom, and those who seek awakening for the sake of all beings. Each stage, it says, rests on the one before, the way a second floor rests on a first. Tibetan teachers later built long teachings on the stages of the path on that frame, and his close Tibetan student, Dromtonpa, gathered his followers into the Kadampa tradition. Fourth, the thread. Atisha was not alone. In these generations Indian teachers traveled north and Tibetan translators traveled south to study, and the learning of the Indian monasteries crossed the mountains in their heads and in their luggage. Tibetan lineages still keep the names, teacher to student, back to the halls of India. Behind a teaching given in Tibet today stands a chain of people, and some of the links were monks at Vikramashila.
screen: `VIKRAMASHILA: A ROYAL MONASTERY.` · `ATISHA, A SENIOR TEACHER.` · `THE LAMP: THREE KINDS OF PEOPLE.` · `TEACHER TO STUDENT, NAME BY NAME.` · then, large: `A CHAIN OF TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who taught you something that mattered, a parent, a coach, a friend, an old boss, then step back one link: who taught them? A grandmother, a mentor, a book they loved; hold that person in mind for a few breaths. If you pray, you can thank them in your own way, and if not, simply let the thanks travel back along the chain.
Atisha. The senior teacher at Vikramashila who crossed the mountains to teach in Tibet until he died there. Today's word.
Your line: the last Indian masters. Their learning lived on in the people they taught. Rest well.

howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism a teaching is usually received through a lineage, and students often learn the names of the teachers who handed it down; Atisha's three kinds of people still frame Tibetan teachings on the stages of the path.
